answer:
In its first edition (1771), the *Encyclopaedia Britannica* counted **six primary planets** — Mercury, Venus, the Earth, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn — circling the Sun in the Copernican arrangement [EB:1771-v1-p489] [EB:1771-v1-p491].

By its eighth edition (1853) Britannica itself had caught up with two major discoveries: **Uranus** (Herschel, 1781) and **Neptune** (Le Verrier and Adams, 1846) [EB:1853-v4-p12].

Modern Wikipedia lists **eight planets**, matching the 1853 Britannica on the major planets [WP:Solar_System#planets]. The main later change is Pluto: discovered in 1930, counted as the ninth planet, and reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006 [WP:Pluto#classification].

- **Knowledge change:** 6 → 8 planets (plus dwarf planets).
- **Perspective change:** the 1771 text reads the system as proof of the Creator's wisdom; Wikipedia calls heliocentrism a superseded model [WP:Heliocentrism].
- **The pictures changed too:** the 1771 plate engraves six orbits about the Sun as a mathematical figure; the modern diagram shows eight planets plus dwarf planets, in colour [EB:1771-v1-p489] [WP:Solar_System#planets].
- One claim about Saturn's rings in the 1771 edition could not be verified [EB:1771-v1-p493].

citations.title: ASTRONOMY — Of the Solar System
citations.snippet: The solar system consists of the sun, and the planets and comets moving about him. The planets are six in number: Mercury, Venus, the Earth, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.

citations.title: ASTRONOMY — Of the Systems of the World
citations.snippet: The Ptolemaic system, which placed the earth immoveable in the centre, is now universally exploded; the Copernican, which places the sun in the centre, is demonstrated to be the true system of the world.

citations.title: ASTRONOMY — Discovery of New Planets
citations.snippet: In 1781 Sir William Herschel discovered the planet Uranus; and in 1846 the planet Neptune was found in the place assigned to it by the calculations of Le Verrier and Adams.

citations.title: Solar System
citations.snippet: The Solar System consists of the Sun and the objects that orbit it. It has eight planets: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.

citations.title: Pluto
citations.snippet: Pluto was discovered in 1930 and was considered the ninth planet until 2006, when the IAU reclassified it as a dwarf planet.

citations.title: Heliocentrism
citations.snippet: Heliocentrism is a superseded astronomical model in which the Earth and planets revolve around the Sun at the center of the universe. Copernicus presented the mathematical model in 1543.

args.question: How many planets are engraved on this plate, and what does the caption say?

vision.question: How many planets are engraved on this plate, and what does the caption say?
vision.answer: Plate XL, headed “THE SOLAR SYSTEM” and signed “A. Bell sculp.” The sun is drawn at the centre with six concentric orbits, each carrying one planet labelled in italic: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn, Saturn being the outermost. The caption reads: “Fig. 1. The Copernican or Solar System, with the orbits of the six primary planets.” No seventh planet, no moons and no comets are engraved.

args.question: How do the 1771 plate and the modern Wikipedia illustration depict the solar system differently?

vision.question: How do the 1771 plate and the modern Wikipedia illustration depict the solar system differently?
vision.answer: Image 1 is a copper engraving: the Sun as a small dark disc with six concentric circular orbits drawn to scale-free, evenly spaced radii, the planets as black dots labelled Mercury to Saturn. Image 2 is a modern colour diagram: the Sun as a large glowing body at the left, eight planets in a row with their relative sizes, and Pluto marked separately as a dwarf planet. The engraving shows the geometry of the orbits; the modern image shows the bodies themselves and adds Uranus and Neptune.
